components.name: OWASP Threat Model Library example builder
Integrated Development Environment (IDE)
components.description: The software environment where code is written and tested—an attack surface due to risks like malicious extensions, insecure settings, or credential exposure.

components.name: Code Assistant Plugin
components.description: A compromised or intentionally malicious AI-powered IDE plugin that appears to assist with coding but performs unauthorized actions—introducing risks such as data exfiltration, credential harvesting, backdoor insertion, or manipulation of code and outputs.

components.name: Local Codebase Clone
components.description: A developer's local copy of a repository—treated as a sensitive asset since it may contain proprietary code, secrets, or configurations that could be exposed if the endpoint is compromised.

components.name: Authentication Service
components.description: The service for verifying the identity of a user or system—risks include credential theft, weak authentication mechanisms, and session hijacking.

components.name: Authorization Service
components.description: The service for determining what an authenticated user or system is allowed to access or perform—risks include excessive permissions, privilege escalation, and misconfigured access controls.

components.name: Third Party MCP Server
components.description: An organization-operated MCP server that integrates the assistant with internal third-party services. Poses risks if misconfigured or inadequately secured, including unauthorized data access, insecure API exposure, and privilege escalation through service integrations.

components.name: Code Assistant Agent
components.description: The agent embedded within the Code Assistant Plugin and running inside the IDE on the developer's workstation. Modeled as a static component prior to plugin activation; once activated it becomes an actor with agency. Handles low-latency tasks such as inline completions and prompt assembly, and invokes local MCP servers for context retrieval. Subject to prompt injection, supply chain compromise via the plugin delivery path, and abuse of IDE-accessible APIs.

components.name: Agentic Framework (Internal)
components.description: The orchestration layer that coordinates multi-step, tool-using workflows on behalf of the assistant. Manages execution flow between the model, retrieval systems, and external services—a high-impact trust boundary where prompt injection, tool misuse, or unintended action chains can have significant consequences.

components.name: Agentic Framework (External SaaS)
components.description: The orchestration layer that coordinates multi-step, tool-using workflows on behalf of the assistant. Manages execution flow between the model, retrieval systems, and external services—a high-impact trust boundary where prompt injection, tool misuse, or unintended action chains can have significant consequences.

components.name: Local Code Assistant Model
components.description: The core AI model that generates responses or code suggestions, run locally (e.g., a self-hosted model). Relevant in threat modeling due to risks like prompt injection, data leakage, model manipulation, and insecure output generation. This is a component within the Agent.

components.name: Remote Code Assistant Model
components.description: The core AI model that generates responses or code suggestions, run remotely (e.g., a cloud-hosted model such as a 30B-parameter model). Relevant in threat modeling due to risks like prompt injection, data leakage, model manipulation, and insecure output generation. This is a component within the Agent.

components.name: Local RAG
components.description: A component, hosted locally, that dynamically fetches relevant content from available data sources to augment the model's context and improve response quality. Introduces risks around ingestion of untrusted or manipulated content, exposure of sensitive data through retrieval, and injection of malicious inputs that propagate into model outputs.

components.name: Remote RAG
components.description: A component, hosted remotely, that dynamically fetches relevant content from available data sources to augment the model's context and improve response quality. Introduces risks around ingestion of untrusted or manipulated content, exposure of sensitive data through retrieval, and injection of malicious inputs that propagate into model outputs.

components.name: Local Context Store
components.description: A locally hosted data store that supplies structured or unstructured content to the model or retrieval pipeline to enrich responses. Risks include unauthorized access to sensitive stored content, poisoning of the data corpus, and data leakage via model outputs.

components.name: Remote Context Store
components.description: A remotely hosted data store that supplies structured or unstructured content to the model or retrieval pipeline to enrich responses. Risks include unauthorized access to sensitive stored content, poisoning of the data corpus, and data leakage via model outputs.

components.name: MCP Gateway
components.description: The ingress service (e.g., proxy, API gateway, or firewall) that receives and routes inbound connections to the assistant backend. Acts as a perimeter trust boundary—misconfiguration or compromise can expose backend infrastructure to unauthorized access or traffic manipulation.

components.name: MCP Server — Agentic SaaS
components.description: The MCP server component hosted within the Agentic SaaS platform, responsible for exposing assistant capabilities and orchestrating downstream agent, model, and retrieval components. A high-value target due to its central role—risks include unauthorized access, data interception, and abuse of its broad orchestration capabilities.

components.name: External Plugin Marketplace
components.description: An externally operated third-party platform where developers discover and install IDE plugins or extensions—introduces supply chain risks such as malicious or vulnerable plugins, insufficient vetting, and potential for unauthorized data access or exfiltration.

components.name: Agentic SaaS
components.description: An externally operated platform that delivers agentic assistant capabilities as a managed service. Introduces risks related to third-party data handling, limited visibility into model behavior and data flows, dependency on external availability, and reduced control over security posture.

components.name: MCP Server — Cloud Service
components.description: A vendor-operated MCP server that integrates the assistant with external cloud platforms and services. Introduces supply chain risks including vulnerable or malicious dependencies, excessive permissions, and potential exfiltration of data passed through the integration.

components.name: Cloud Service (AWS/GCP/etc.)
components.description: Third-party infrastructure and cloud service providers used as dependencies or execution targets—introduce additional risks including supply chain vulnerabilities, data exposure, and limited visibility or control over security practices.

blueprints.name: Code Assistant
blueprints.description: An AI-powered development assistant surfaced to a developer inside an IDE as a model plugin. The assistant embeds agent capabilities directly into the editing experience, supporting both a fully local deployment (Sub Use Case 1a) and a remote SaaS-hosted agentic framework (Sub Use Case 1b).

scope.name: Code Assistant
scope.description: The Code Assistant use case describes an AI-powered development assistant that is surfaced to a developer directly inside an Integrated Development Environment (IDE). The assistant is installed as a model plugin — a first-class IDE extension that embeds agent capabilities into the editing experience without requiring the developer to switch context to a separate application.

zones.name: Internal
zones.description: Represents locally networked resources: the developer's workstation, the IDE, the Code Assistant Plugin and its embedded agent, the local agentic framework, and any MCP servers reachable within the organization's local network. All components within this boundary are subject to the organization's own security controls.

zones.name: External SaaS
zones.description: Represents remotely networked managed services: the Agentic SaaS platform (e.g., Claude Code, Cursor), the External Plugin Marketplace, and any third-party application services accessed over the public internet. Components within this boundary operate under a third-party trust model with limited organizational visibility.

zones.name: External Cloud
zones.description: Represents remotely networked cloud infrastructure providers: AWS, GCP, Azure, and similar platforms accessed via MCP Servers. Components within this boundary are governed by the cloud provider's shared-responsibility model.

persona.description: Human actor who writes, modifies, and maintains code—considered a potential target (e.g., phishing, credential theft) or source of risk (e.g., introducing vulnerabilities or misconfigurations).

actors.description: The human developer who interacts with the code assistant within the IDE.

The agent (local, dynamic) delivered as part of the Code Assistant Plugin. Operates as a static component prior to installation; once activated in the IDE it becomes an actor with agency over the developer environment. Local: the agent and its agentic framework run entirely on the developer's workstation within the internal trust boundary. Dynamic: the agent can take autonomous actions — tool calling, invoking MCP servers, and orchestrating multi-step workflows. A context store is available for structured state across steps. A RAG pipeline exists in the architecture but is not exercised in the current use case variants and is deferred for later consideration. Susceptible to prompt injection, workflow hijacking, and cascading misuse of MCP-accessible services.

The agent (remote, dynamic) hosted entirely within the External SaaS trust boundary, opaque to the developer beyond its API surface. Remote: the agent and its agentic framework operate outside the developer's workstation within a third-party platform. Dynamic: the agent can take autonomous actions — tool calling, invoking MCP servers, and orchestrating multi-step workflows. May access additional tools, skills, and connectors not enumerated in this use case. Susceptible to prompt injection via remote context, third-party data handling risks, and limited developer visibility into its internal operations.

useCases.name: Code Assistant
useCases.description: A developer uses an AI-powered code assistant—composed of a plugin, one or more agents, a language model, a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline, and an agentic framework—to accelerate software development tasks such as code generation, explanation, and review. The assistant may run fully on the developer's workstation (Sub Use Case 1a) or offload its agentic components to an external SaaS platform (Sub Use Case 1b).
preconditions: Developer has an IDE installed and a local codebase clone available.

The Code Assistant Plugin has been installed from a trusted, authenticated Plugin Marketplace (e.g., VS Code Marketplace, JetBrains Marketplace) whose publisher identity and plugin integrity are verified before delivery to the IDE.
The installed Code Assistant Plugin is authenticated and authorized via the Authentication and Authorization Services.
The MCP Server — Agentic SaaS (e.g., Claude Code, hosted remotely on the Agentic SaaS platform) is reachable from the developer's workstation.
The locally installed MCP Server (e.g., a Jira MCP Server installed on the developer's workstation) is running and reachable.
postconditions: Developer receives AI-generated code suggestions, completions, or reviews.
Any tool invocations performed by agents are logged and auditable.
No sensitive code or credentials are unintentionally exfiltrated.

exceptions.name: Authentication Failure
exceptions.condition: The Authentication Service rejects the Developer's credentials or token.
exceptions.description: The developer cannot authenticate, preventing plugin activation.
exceptions.handling: The plugin displays an authentication error; the developer is prompted to re-authenticate or contact an administrator.

exceptions.name: MCP Server Unreachable
exceptions.condition: An internal or external MCP Server is unavailable or returns a connection error.
exceptions.description: Tool calls from the agent cannot be completed, potentially stalling multi-step workflows.
exceptions.handling: The agent reports the tool failure to the developer and falls back to model-only responses where possible.

exceptions.name: Prompt Injection Detected
exceptions.condition: Malicious content in the codebase, context store, or RAG output attempts to redirect agent behavior.
exceptions.description: An injected instruction overrides the developer's intent, potentially causing unauthorized tool invocations or data exfiltration.
exceptions.handling: The agentic framework applies input sanitization; suspicious instructions are flagged and execution is halted pending developer review.

successCriteria: Developer receives accurate, contextually relevant code suggestions or completions.
All agent tool invocations are authorized and within the defined permission scope.
No sensitive data (credentials, proprietary code) is transmitted to unauthorized endpoints.
Audit logs capture all agent actions and external service calls.
notes: This top-level use case is realized by two sub use cases (1a and 1b) that differ in the deployment location of the Agentic Framework and its hosted components.

useCases.name: Code Assistant — Sub Use Case 1a (Local Agentic Framework)
useCases.description: The developer's workstation hosts the full agentic framework, including the dynamic agent, model, RAG pipeline, and context store. The assistant plugin communicates directly with locally running components. MCP Servers bridge internal third-party services and external cloud platforms.
preconditions: The developer's workstation has sufficient resources to run the local Code Assistant Model (e.g., an 8B-parameter model).
The Agentic Framework, RAG pipeline, and Context Store are installed and running locally.
The Code Assistant Plugin is installed in the IDE and authenticated.
Internal MCP Server and relevant Third Party Services are reachable.
External Cloud MCP Server is reachable if cloud service integrations are required.
postconditions: Developer receives AI-generated code suggestions produced by the locally hosted model.
All data—including codebase content and context—remains within the internal network boundary unless explicitly forwarded via MCP to an external cloud service.
Agent tool invocations are logged locally.

exceptions.name: Insufficient Local Resources
exceptions.condition: The workstation does not have enough CPU/GPU/RAM to run the local model.
exceptions.description: Model inference fails or produces degraded responses due to resource constraints.
exceptions.handling: The framework reports an error to the developer; the developer may reduce model size or free system resources.

exceptions.name: Context Store Poisoning
exceptions.condition: Malicious or manipulated content is present in the Local Context Store.
exceptions.description: Poisoned retrieval data is injected into the model prompt, potentially altering agent behavior.
exceptions.handling: The RAG pipeline applies content validation; suspicious documents are flagged and excluded from context assembly.

successCriteria: Code suggestions are generated entirely within the internal trust boundary.
No developer code or credentials are transmitted to unapproved external endpoints.
Agent tool calls are restricted to permitted MCP Servers.
Local model inference completes within an acceptable latency threshold.
notes: This sub use case is characterized by a fully local agentic stack — the dynamic agent, model, RAG, and context store all run on the developer's workstation.
MCP Servers act as the sole egress path to third-party and cloud services.

useCases.name: Code Assistant — Sub Use Case 1b (External SaaS Agentic Framework)
useCases.description: The agentic framework is offloaded to an external SaaS platform, which hosts the dynamic agent, model, RAG pipeline, and context store behind an MCP Gateway. The workstation retains the Code Assistant Plugin and local agent. MCP Servers connect to both internal third-party services and external cloud platforms. The Plugin Marketplace is the source for plugin installation.
preconditions: The Code Assistant Plugin is installed from the External Plugin Marketplace and is authenticated.
The Agentic SaaS platform is accessible and the developer's account is provisioned.
The MCP Gateway on the Agentic SaaS platform is reachable from the developer's workstation.
Internal MCP Server and relevant Third Party Services (e.g., Jira, GitHub) are reachable.
External Cloud MCP Server is reachable if cloud service integrations are required.
postconditions: Developer receives AI-generated code suggestions produced by the remotely hosted model.
Developer code and context submitted to the SaaS platform are governed by the platform's data handling and retention policies.
Agent tool invocations on the SaaS side are logged by the platform.

exceptions.name: Agentic SaaS Platform Unavailable
exceptions.condition: The Agentic SaaS platform or MCP Gateway is unreachable due to an outage or network failure.
exceptions.description: The developer cannot complete multi-step agentic tasks; the plugin degrades to static-only responses.
exceptions.handling: The Code Assistant Agent (local, dynamic) notifies the developer of the degraded state and provides best-effort responses without SaaS delegation.

exceptions.name: Malicious Plugin from Marketplace
exceptions.condition: A plugin installed from the External Plugin Marketplace contains malicious code.
exceptions.description: The plugin exfiltrates developer credentials, codebase content, or manipulates agent outputs.

Below is the structured MITRE CAPEC / CWE mapping for the scenario.

---

## Assumed attack flow (step-by-step)

* **Attacker role:** External attacker (malicious dependency maintainer or compromised third-party maintainer account)
* **Delivery mechanism:** Third-party dependency inclusion via plugin dependency resolution (package manager / build system)
* **What is modified:** Runtime behavior (malicious native library loaded/executed by the plugin)
* **How malicious behavior is triggered:** Automatic plugin execution context → native library load → privilege escalation condition (no user prompt required)

---

## the attacker’s strategy (distribution + deception + supply chain)

**CAPEC-435 (Supply Chain Compromise)** — The attacker compromises the software supply chain by inserting malicious code into a third-party dependency consumed by the plugin.

**CAPEC-442 (Third-Party Component Inclusion)** — The attack succeeds through inclusion of a malicious external native library as a trusted dependency.

**CAPEC-419 (Malicious Logic Insertion)** — The attacker embeds deliberate malicious functionality (privilege escalation logic) into the library.

**CAPEC-148 (Content Spoofing)** — The malicious library presents itself as a legitimate dependency to evade detection and trust checks.

> **Explicit class handling:**
>
> * **Supply-chain compromise:** included (primary vector).
> * **Malicious logic insertion:** included (native payload).
> * **Backdoor / hidden functionality:** *included implicitly* via CAPEC-419 (logic is hidden in native code).
> * **Data/instruction manipulation:** rejected (code execution, not data poisoning).
> * **Execution without user intent:** included (plugin auto-load behavior).

---

## the execution and impact

**CAPEC-233 (Privilege Escalation)** — The malicious native library exploits execution context to gain elevated local privileges.

**CAPEC-94 (Code Injection)** — Malicious native code is executed within the plugin’s process context.

**CAPEC-641 (Execution of Unauthorized Code)** — The system executes attacker-controlled native code without user authorization.

---

## the underlying trust failure

**CWE-829 (Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere)** — Untrusted third-party native code is trusted and executed as part of the plugin.

**CWE-345 (Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity)** — No authenticity validation of dependency origin or maintainer identity.

Assumed Attack Flow
This breakdown serves as the scenario logic (TL;DR):

Attacker Role: External Threat Actor (Supply Chain Interdiction). The attacker does not need direct access to the plugin developer’s internal systems but targets the upstream ecosystem.

Delivery Mechanism: Compromised Third-Party Dependency (Upstream Source). The attacker injects the malicious native library into a legitimate package (e.g., via a compromised maintainer account or repo hijack) which is then pulled by the plugin's build process.

What is Modified: Runtime Behavior / Binary Artifacts. The source code or binary distribution of the dependency now contains a shared object/DLL with an embedded payload.

Trigger: Plugin Execution / Runtime Loading. The malicious behavior executes automatically when the AI coding assistant plugin initializes the dependency or calls a specific function within the native library.

the attacker’s strategy (distribution + deception + supply chain):
CAPEC-438 (Modification during Manufacture) — The attacker successfully alters the dependency's build artifacts or source code prior to distribution, ensuring the "malicious native library" is compiled and included as a standard component.

CAPEC-439 (Manipulation during Distribution) — Considered but subordinate to 438 in this specific framing: While the distribution channel delivers the code, the core success lies in the modification of the artifact (the library) itself before the plugin developer consumes it.

CAPEC-538 (Open Source Supply Chain Compromise) — Rejected for specificity: While highly relevant if the dependency is open source, CAPEC-438 describes the technical action (modification) more precisely than the campaign type (open source), fitting the "strategy of insertion" requirement better.

the execution and impact:
CAPEC-549 (Local Privilege Escalation) — The native library exploits the execution context (or a vulnerability in the host OS) to elevate the plugin's process permissions from user-level to administrative/root level.

CAPEC-262 (Execution of Code) — Rejected for redundancy: This is implicit in privilege escalation. We focus on the impact (LPE) rather than the generic action of running code.

the underlying trust failure:
CWE-1357 (Reliance on Insufficiently Trustworthy Component) — The primary systemic failure is the architectural decision to integrate a third-party dependency without sufficient verification of its integrity or provenance.

CWE-829 (Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere) — This describes the specific mechanical failure where the application imports code (the native library) from a source (the dependency repo) that is outside the developer's direct control.

CAPEC suggestion (ChatGPT, needs checking):
the attacker’s strategy (distribution + deception + supply chain):

CAPEC-22 (Exploiting Trust in Client) — The MCP service implicitly trusts the remote peer / message and processes attacker-controlled requests as if they were from a valid client, enabling abuse of the connection channel.

the execution and impact:

CAPEC-88 (OS Command Injection) — The attacker’s crafted MCP payload causes the server to execute attacker-supplied OS commands (remote code execution), compromising system integrity.

the underlying trust failure:

CWE-306 (Missing Authentication for Critical Function) — The MCP endpoint performs sensitive actions without requiring a provable identity, allowing unauthenticated remote triggering of dangerous functionality.

CWE-20 (Improper Input Validation) — The MCP handler accepts attacker-controlled input without enforcing required safety properties/format, enabling malicious payloads to reach sinks.

CWE-78 (Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command) — The server constructs/executes OS commands using externally influenced input without proper neutralization, enabling command execution.

Explicitly considered classes (include / reject)

Supply-chain compromise: Rejected (attack is direct exploitation over an MCP connection; no component/update distribution is required).

Malicious logic insertion: Rejected (no implanted logic; the system’s existing vulnerable logic is abused).

Backdoor / hidden functionality: Rejected (RCE comes from exploitation, not a deliberately hidden access path).

Data or instruction manipulation: Included (attacker manipulates protocol input to alter program interpretation, culminating in injection/execution).

Execution without user intent: Included (server executes commands as a side effect of handling a network request, with no legitimate user intention for those commands).

CAPEC suggestion (ChatGPT, needs checking):
the attacker’s strategy (distribution + deception + supply chain):

CAPEC-446 (Malicious Logic Insertion into Product Software via Inclusion of 3rd Party Component Dependency) — attacker ships/updates an agent plugin/dependency that “helpfully” captures/forwards tokens (e.g., to logs/telemetry or to another service) to cross the trust boundary.

CAPEC-445 (Malicious Logic Insertion into Product Software via Configuration Management Manipulation) — attacker compromises CI/CD or config management so the agent build/deploy includes token-exfiltrating logic even if the source repo looks clean.

CAPEC-669 (Alteration of a Software Update) — attacker tampers with an update channel so an agent/runtime update introduces secret-handling changes (e.g., enabling verbose logging or exporting memory containing tokens).

CAPEC-523 (Malicious Software Implanted) — attacker implants hidden functionality/backdoor in agent tooling that silently retains or exfiltrates secrets for later unauthorized access.

the execution and impact:

CAPEC-593 (Session Hijacking) — attacker uses stolen session material (session token/cookie) to act as the victim/service identity and access resources the attacker shouldn’t.

CAPEC-60 (Reusing Session IDs (aka Session Replay)) — attacker replays a captured session ID/access token to re-enter privileged flows (including agent tool calls) without re-authentication.

CAPEC-633 (Token Impersonation) — attacker forges/creates/uses a token to impersonate a different entity, enabling privilege escalation when downstream components trust the token blindly.

CAPEC-21 (Exploitation of Trusted Identifiers) — attacker “rides” trusted identifiers (session IDs/cookies/tokens) passed/stored across internal boundaries to perform authorized actions under a stolen identity (this is broader, but is the best-fit CAPEC umbrella for “trusted token reused across trust boundaries,” especially between agents).

the underlying trust failure:

CWE-522 (Insufficiently Protected Credentials) — tokens/secrets are stored or transmitted in a way that allows interception/retrieval (e.g., placed into agent prompts, inter-agent messages, or tool-call payloads without proper protection).

CWE-532 (Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File) — agent/runtime/debug logging captures tokens (headers, cookies, bearer tokens) so anyone with log access can hijack sessions.

CWE-201 (Insertion of Sensitive Information Into Sent Data) — agent sends secrets across a boundary to another actor (another agent, LLM provider, plugin service, or downstream tool) that should not receive them.
